book: How Search Decides What You See
author: Aaron Tay

episodes.title: Two search scouts, one result list
episodes.subtitle: Why hybrid retrieval exists

scenes.title: One question. Two different scouts.
scenes.claim: Different retrieval routes preserve different evidence
scenes.narration: Imagine a library floating in space. Two search scouts explore it. One follows indexed words. The other follows learnt coordinates. They can discover different useful records for the same question. Chapter ten asks how we combine what they bring home.

scenes.title: Sometimes one tiny symbol matters
scenes.claim: Schematic example: exact identifiers can matter
scenes.narration: Suppose you need the exact identifier Z X forty one. A lexical route can preserve its analysed term evidence. A dense representation may blur it with a similar identifier. This is a teaching illustration, not a measured result. The actual analysis rules and model still matter.

scenes.title: Sometimes the useful words are different
scenes.claim: A dense route can bridge different formulations
scenes.narration: Now ask whether you are being delulu about a job. A passage about unrealistic employment expectations might be useful without sharing the distinctive slang. A trained dense retriever can bridge formulations. An unexpanded lexical search may miss that connection. Neither route has a monopoly on relevance.

scenes.title: Their blind spots can complement each other
scenes.claim: Two lists → a candidate union → a combination rule
scenes.narration: Running both scouts creates two candidate lists. Their union may include relevant records that either route misses alone. But duplicate records need a consistent identity, and the combined candidates still need an order. More routes create an opportunity, not an automatic improvement.

scenes.title: Count the routes. Then follow the stages.
scenes.claim: BM25 → reranker: multi-stage, with one candidate route
scenes.narration: Hybrid and multi-stage describe different things. B M twenty five followed by a cross-encoder reranker has several stages, but only one candidate-generation route. Hybrid means combining candidates or scores from multiple retrieval routes. A single scoring stage can blend lexical and dense evidence too.

scenes.title: Two lists can meet at a fusion stage
scenes.claim: Parallel lexical + dense retrieval → fusion
scenes.narration: In this arrangement, lexical and dense retrieval run in parallel. Fusion combines the lists into one ranking. That makes it hybrid, and the separate fusion step also makes this arrangement multi-stage. It does not require a reranker. Reciprocal Rank Fusion is one possible combination rule.

scenes.title: A reranker can inspect the fused shortlist
scenes.claim: Two routes → fusion → reranking
scenes.narration: We can add a later reranker to compare the fused shortlist more carefully. This pipeline is both hybrid and multi-stage. But the reranker can only reorder the candidates supplied to it. A record missed by both scouts never arrives at this desk.

scenes.title: A label cannot explain a result
scenes.claim: Ask: which routes, what depth, which fusion rule?
scenes.narration: When a product says hybrid search, ask which routes ran, how many records each supplied, how duplicates were handled, and how the evidence was combined. Then evaluate the results for your task. The next film opens one simple fusion rule and follows every contribution.

episodes.title: When ranks become votes
episodes.subtitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion, step by step

scenes.title: The same records, in two orders
scenes.claim: Chapter example: lexical A, B, C · dense C, A, D
scenes.narration: Our lexical scout returns A, B, C. Our dense scout returns C, A, D. These letters identify the same records wherever they appear. Reciprocal Rank Fusion, or R R F, will turn these two rankings into one. The letters are schematic, with no relevance judgements attached.

scenes.title: Raw scores speak different languages
scenes.claim: RRF uses positions, rather than raw retrieval scores
scenes.narration: A B M twenty five score and a vector similarity score do not share a natural scale. Simply adding them can be misleading. R R F sidesteps that problem. It ignores the raw scores and uses each record's rank position in each supplied list.

scenes.title: Each appearance makes a contribution
scenes.claim: RRF(d) = sum of 1 / (c + rank) over supplied lists
scenes.narration: For every list containing a record, take one divided by a constant plus its rank. Add those contributions. A record absent from a supplied list adds zero from that list. The chapter uses c equals sixty. This constant is separate from the number of results returned.

scenes.title: Follow A through the calculation
scenes.narration: A is first in the lexical list, so it contributes one over sixty one. A is second in the dense list, adding one over sixty two. Together, that is approximately zero point zero three two five two. One record, two appearances, one total.

scenes.title: Agreement near the top is rewarded
scenes.claim: Fused order at c = 60: A → C → B → D
scenes.narration: C combines third place and first place, finishing just behind A. B appears only in the lexical list, and D only in the dense list. Their single contributions are smaller here. The fused order is A, C, B, D. Outside a supplied list does not mean irrelevant.

scenes.title: The constant softens the top-rank advantage
scenes.claim: 60 is conventional; c is not input depth or output depth
scenes.narration: A larger constant makes neighbouring positions contribute more similarly. Compare the first and third positions with c equal to one, then sixty. Sixty is a conventional setting, not a universal law. The best setting still depends on the task, collection, and retrieval setup.

scenes.title: Ranks discard the distance between scores
scenes.claim: Same positions → same RRF contributions, even with different gaps
scenes.narration: Here is the price of simplicity. One ranking has a tiny score gap between first and second. Another has an enormous gap. R R F sees the same positions, so it gives the same contributions. Once scores become ranks, their original gaps disappear.

scenes.title: No appearance means no contribution
scenes.claim: Input cutoffs determine what fusion can see
scenes.narration: Fusion sees only the supplied lists. A useful record below both input cutoffs gets no contribution at all. Asking fusion to return more records cannot recover it. R R F is a useful baseline, not a relevance model or a guarantee of improvement. Test it on the searches that matter.

episodes.title: Blend every time, or choose a route?
episodes.subtitle: The decisions hidden inside hybrid search

scenes.title: Two controls. Two different decisions.
scenes.claim: Routing chooses paths · fusion combines their results
scenes.narration: A search system has two separate controls. One decides which retrieval paths will run. The other decides how returned evidence becomes one ranking. Confusing those controls makes a hybrid label hard to interpret. Let's follow the question through each decision.

scenes.title: A blend runs prescribed routes
scenes.claim: Run both prescribed paths, then combine their outputs
scenes.narration: A fixed blend runs its prescribed lexical and dense routes, then combines their outputs. The same types of evidence can compete on every query. A parser may first transform the question, but parsing alone does not make the search hybrid. Combining retrieval evidence does.

scenes.title: A router chooses paths for this query
scenes.claim: Lexical, dense, or both: the decision can vary by query
scenes.narration: A router can choose lexical retrieval for one question, dense retrieval for another, and both for a third. A run using one path combines nothing, under this book's definition of hybrid. If both paths return lists, the system still needs a rule to combine them.

scenes.title: Routing alone does not establish agency
scenes.claim: A rule, classifier, or model can select a retrieval route
scenes.narration: A routing decision might come from a rule, a classifier, or a model. That decision alone does not prove the system is agentic. Choosing the initial path is separate from an agent deciding subsequent actions. To explain a result, first expose which evidence was allowed to compete.

scenes.title: Input depth and output depth are different
scenes.claim: Two lists of depth 3 → four unique candidates → output top 2
scenes.narration: Return to the chapter's toy lists. Three records from each route produce four unique candidates. Returning only the top two hides B and D at presentation. Reducing the input lists changes the evidence fusion receives. These are different boundaries. The constant sixty is neither boundary.

scenes.title: Equal routes are a choice, too
scenes.claim: Weighted variant: sum of w / (c + rank)
scenes.narration: Standard R R F gives the lists equal weight. An implementation can add explicit route weights. In our toy example, doubling the dense weight moves C above A. That calculated change does not prove better relevance. Weights should reflect evaluated choices, not faith in a route.

scenes.title: Fusion can combine query variants, too
scenes.claim: Several query variants → ranked lists → RRF
scenes.narration: R R F is a list-combination rule, so its inputs need not come from different retrieval methods. Several reformulations of one question can each produce a ranking from the same retriever. Fusion can merge those rankings too. Using R R F therefore does not, by itself, demonstrate lexical and dense hybrid retrieval.

scenes.title: Make the hidden choices testable
scenes.claim: Compare routes and fusion on a locally judged query set
scenes.narration: Build a small set of representative questions and known useful records. Compare lexical retrieval, dense retrieval, and the combined system at stated cutoffs. Inspect misses, duplicates, and changes in order. Hybrid is a design space. Its value comes from evidence on your collection, for your users' tasks.
